solution.concept_anchor: Swaran Singh Committee recommendations vs. actual adoption
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students often conflate the Swaran Singh Committee's specific recommendations (8 duties, sanctions, separate chapter) with what was actually incorporated into the Constitution.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Swaran Singh Committee recommended 8 duties — the 42nd Amendment actually inserted 10 duties (clauses a–j), not the same number as recommended.
Eliminate (c): The Committee recommended that sanctions be prescribed for breach — this was NOT adopted; FDs remain non-justiciable without penal enforcement.
Eliminate (d): The Committee recommended a separate chapter — instead, FDs were placed within Part IV-A as a single article (51A), not a separate Part.

Confirm (b): The Committee's recommendation that fundamental duties be incorporated as part of the constitutional framework was accepted — but the specific details (number, sanctions, separate chapter) were modified.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the gap between what the Swaran Singh Committee recommended and what was actually enacted. Students who have read about the Committee typically remember it 'recommended Fundamental Duties' and assume all details were adopted. In reality, the Committee recommended 8 duties (42nd Amendment inserted 10), recommended sanctions for breach (not adopted — FDs remain non-justiciable), and recommended a separate chapter (instead placed as Part IV-A). The correct answer targets the one thing that WAS accepted: the principle of including duties in the Constitution.

upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in the fact that the Swaran Singh Committee's specific recommendations differed substantially from what was actually adopted. The Committee recommended 8 duties — but 10 were inserted. It recommended sanctions — but none were prescribed. It recommended a separate chapter — but Part IV-A was added instead. A student who only knows 'Swaran Singh Committee recommended FDs' will be unable to identify which specific element was or was not adopted.
final_explanation:
The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) was tasked with recommending the inclusion of fundamental duties in the Constitution. Its recommendations formed the basis for the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, which inserted Article 51A. However, the adoption was selective.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Committee recommended 8 duties; the 42nd Amendment actually inserted 10 duties (clauses a through j). The number was changed.
• Option (b) — Correct: The broad principle of incorporating citizen duties was accepted, but specific details were modified.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Committee recommended that sanctions be prescribed for breach of duties. This was NOT adopted — Fundamental Duties remain non-justiciable and carry no direct penal consequence.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Committee recommended a separate chapter entirely; instead, Part IV-A was added as a single article (51A) appended after Part IV.

Value Addition:
• The 11th duty (clause k) was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment, 2002 — the Swaran Singh Committee had no role in this.
• Part IV-A placement is deliberate — FDs are neither rights (Part III) nor state directives (Part IV).
• India borrowed the concept of codified citizen duties from the USSR Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Applicability of Fundamental Duties — citizens only

statement_analysis.statement: All eleven Fundamental Duties under Article 51A apply exclusively to Indian citizens and do not extend to foreigners residing in India.
statement_analysis.reason: This statement is factually accurate — unlike Fundamental Rights such as Articles 14 and 21 which apply to 'all persons,' Article 51A applies only to citizens.

statement_analysis.statement: Since Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution apply to all persons including foreigners, Fundamental Duties must similarly be construed to apply to all persons within India's territory.
statement_analysis.reason: The scope of Fundamental Rights is independent of the scope of Fundamental Duties — the constitutional text of Article 51A explicitly addresses citizens, and there is no interpretive basis to extend duties to non-citizens merely because some rights apply universally.

statement_analysis.statement: Clause (k) of Article 51A, which concerns educational duties of parents or guardians, applies to citizens in their capacity as parents or guardians and does not extend to non-citizen residents of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Clause (k) is citizen-specific despite being functionally tied to the role of parent/guardian — the duty is on the citizen, not on the role regardless of citizenship.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 2 is wrong may still second-guess Statement 3 if they confuse the 'role-based' nature of clause (k) with a broader applicability.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is factually correct — all 11 FDs apply only to citizens; this statement is NOT incorrect.

Statement 2 is factually incorrect — the universal applicability of Articles 14 and 21 has no bearing on the citizen-specific scope of Article 51A; the question asks which is NOT correct, so Statement 2 qualifies.
Statement 3 is factually correct — clause (k) remains citizen-specific; this statement is NOT incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — select option (b): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the well-known fact that Articles 14 and 21 apply to 'all persons' and tempts students to reason by analogy that duties must also have universal application. This is a scope-extension error — the constitutional text of Article 51A is unambiguously citizen-specific, and cross-provision analogy does not override express textual scope.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A draws a clear citizenship boundary — all eleven Fundamental Duties apply exclusively to Indian citizens. This contrasts with certain Fundamental Rights (Articles 14 and 21) that extend to 'all persons,' including foreigners and corporations.

• Statement 1 — Correct (NOT the answer): All FDs are citizen-specific. Foreigners, corporations, and other juridical persons are not bound by Article 51A.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (this IS the answer): The applicability of Articles 14 and 21 to all persons is a separate constitutional design choice. It cannot be imported to expand the scope of Article 51A, which expressly governs citizens. There is no interpretive rule that mandates parallel scope between rights and duties.
• Statement 3 — Correct (NOT the answer): Clause (k) is role-based (parent/guardian) but remains citizen-specific — a non-citizen parent has no constitutional duty under 51A(k), though the child's right under Article 21A and the State's obligation under the RTE Act may still apply.

Value Addition:
• Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are citizen-specific rights — FDs share this narrower applicability.
• Corporations cannot be duty-bearers under Article 51A.
• The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted both Article 21A (right) and clause (k) (duty) simultaneously.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 48A vs. Article 51A(g) — state vs. citizen environmental duty

statement_analysis.statement: Article 48A of the Constitution directs the State to endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 48A is a Directive Principle of State Policy — it imposes an obligation on the State (not citizens) to protect the environment; it was also inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(g) imposes a duty on every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, AND to have compassion for living creatures.
statement_analysis.reason: 51A(g) explicitly covers forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife and adds the compassion-for-living-creatures obligation — making it a two-part citizen duty distinct from the state-directed Article 48A.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(g) and Article 48A together impose identical obligations — the distinction is only that one applies to citizens and the other to the State.
statement_analysis.reason: The obligations are not identical — Article 48A covers protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding forests and wildlife; Article 51A(g) additionally includes 'compassion for living creatures,' which has no parallel in Article 48A.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court has invoked Article 51A(g) in environmental adjudication to expand the scope of citizen and industrial obligations toward environmental protection.
statement_analysis.reason: In MC Mehta v. Union of India and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, the Supreme Court cited 51A(g) to impose environmental duties and establish the 'polluter pays' principle.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who correctly evaluate the first two pairs as correct may assume Statement 3 is also correct given its superficial plausibility, arriving at 'Only three' without checking the 'identical obligations' claim.
elimination_logic: Pair 1 is correct — Article 48A is a well-known DPSP on environment inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
Pair 2 is correct — Article 51A(g)'s text explicitly includes forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife, and compassion for living creatures.
Pair 3 is incorrect — 51A(g) adds 'compassion for living creatures' which is absent from Article 48A; the obligations are NOT identical.
Pair 4 is correct — MC Mehta and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum cases confirm judicial invocation of 51A(g); three of four pairs are correct, so the answer is (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is designed to exploit conflation between Article 48A and 51A(g). Students familiar with both provisions often summarise them as 'same duty on state and citizen respectively' — but this overlooks the 'compassion for living creatures' element in 51A(g) that has no counterpart in 48A. The question rewards precise textual recall over impressionistic understanding.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 48A and 51A(g) form a complementary pair — one directing the State and the other binding citizens — but they are not textually identical.

• Pair 1 — Correct: Article 48A (DPSP) directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. It was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
• Pair 2 — Correct: Article 51A(g) imposes a two-part citizen duty: (i) protect and improve natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife; (ii) have compassion for living creatures. The second limb is distinct.
• Pair 3 — Incorrect: The obligations are NOT identical. Article 48A does not include 'compassion for living creatures' — this clause appears only in 51A(g). The claim of identical obligations is false.
• Pair 4 — Correct: The Supreme Court has repeatedly invoked 51A(g) — notably in MC Mehta cases and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum — to impose environmental obligations and develop the polluter-pays principle.

Only three of the four pairs/statements are correct — answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Both Articles 48A and 51A(g) were inserted simultaneously by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
• 51A(g) is the ONLY Fundamental Duty with an explicit environmental dimension.
• 'Compassion for living creatures' in 51A(g) is a basis for animal welfare jurisprudence in India.

solution.concept_anchor: Precise content mapping of specific Fundamental Duties
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly places 'humanism' under 51A(h) but swaps 51A(e) and 51A(f), exploiting the fact that both relate to cultural identity and harmony.
elimination_logic: A matches with 3: Article 51A(h) explicitly lists scientific temper, humanism, and spirit of inquiry and reform — 'humanism' is the often-missed component.

B matches with 1: Article 51A(e) deals with harmony and common brotherhood transcending religious, linguistic, regional or sectional diversities AND renouncing practices derogatory to women's dignity.
C matches with 4: Article 51A(f) concerns preserving India's rich heritage of COMPOSITE culture — 'composite' is the precise keyword.
D matches with 2: Article 51A(c) covers upholding sovereignty, unity, AND integrity — all three terms are required; this eliminates options that omit any one of the three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is an entity-swap between 51A(e) and 51A(f). Both involve cultural and social cohesion themes — 51A(e) on brotherhood and renouncing derogatory practices, 51A(f) on composite cultural heritage. Students who have not memorised clause letters precisely will interchange these two. Additionally, 51A(h)'s inclusion of 'humanism' alongside 'scientific temper' is a frequently missed element.
solution.final_explanation:
Matching specific Fundamental Duties to their precise constitutional content requires clause-level precision.

• A–3: Article 51A(h) mandates developing scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform. 'Humanism' is the element most commonly missed in recall — students typically only remember 'scientific temper.'
• B–1: Article 51A(e) requires promoting harmony and common brotherhood transcending religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional diversities, and renouncing practices derogatory to women's dignity. The specific categories listed (religious, linguistic, regional, sectional) are testable.
• C–4: Article 51A(f) specifically uses the word 'composite' to describe Indian cultural heritage — 'preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture.' This is the keyword that distinguishes it from a generic cultural preservation duty.
• D–2: Article 51A(c) lists three obligations: uphold sovereignty, unity, AND integrity of India — all three must be noted; omitting any one makes a statement incorrect.

Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → Option (c).

Value Addition:
• 51A(h) is the only duty with an explicitly epistemological/intellectual character.
• 51A(e)'s 'dignity of women' clause has been cited in triple talaq and sati-related judicial reasoning.
• 'Integrity' was added to the Preamble by the same 42nd Amendment that inserted FDs — constitutional bundling.

solution.concept_anchor: Three-way relationship: Article 21A, Article 51A(k), and RTE Act
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students aware of the non-justiciability of FDs may conclude that the parent has no legal obligation at all, conflating the non-justiciability of the duty as a constitutional claim with the existence of statutory liability under the RTE Act.
elimination_logic: The constitutional duty under 51A(k) is non-justiciable by itself — a parent cannot be dragged to court solely for breaching a Fundamental Duty.
However, the RTE Act, 2009 (which operationalises Article 21A and reinforces 51A(k)) does create statutory obligations — the school authority and the State have enforceable duties under the RTE Act.
The child's RIGHT to free and compulsory education under Article 21A is judicially enforceable — the child or guardian can approach a court to enforce the child's right, not the parent's duty.

The correct framing is: Manish's son's RIGHT under Article 21A is enforceable against the State; Manish's DUTY under 51A(k) is not directly judicially enforceable against him as a constitutional claim — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario conflates the constitutional duty on the parent (51A(k)) with the child's constitutional right (Article 21A) and the state's statutory obligation (RTE Act). Students often assume that because the RTE Act exists, the parent's 51A(k) duty is directly enforceable by a court against the parent. In reality, the RTE Act primarily imposes obligations on the State and school authorities to provide free education, not a penal enforcement of the parent's constitutional duty.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the three-way constitutional architecture created by the 86th Amendment:

Article 21A gives children (6–14 years) a fundamental right to free and compulsory education — enforceable against the STATE. Article 51A(k) places on parent-citizens a duty to provide educational opportunities to their children in this age group — this is a constitutional duty but non-justiciable as a standalone claim. The RTE Act, 2009, operationalises Article 21A by imposing obligations on the State and educational institutions.

In Manish's scenario:
• Option (a) — Incorrect: It is wrong to say Manish has no legal obligation — the RTE Act framework does impose parental responsibilities, though not as a direct constitutional enforcement of 51A(k).
• Option (b) — Correct: The son's right under Article 21A is enforceable against the State; Manish's duty under 51A(k) is non-justiciable as a constitutional claim, but the statutory framework of the RTE Act creates related obligations.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: No court can directly compel Manish to perform his 51A(k) duty through a writ — there is no direct constitutional enforcement mechanism.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Fundamental Duties do not override Fundamental Rights; the child's right is primary.

Value Addition:
• The 86th Amendment simultaneously amended Articles 21A, 45, and 51A — a single amendment creating a triangulated framework.
• Under the RTE Act, schools (not parents) face closure/penalty for non-compliance.
• Article 21A applies to children aged 6–14; the 86th Amendment shifted early childhood care (below 6) to Article 45.

solution.concept_anchor: Duties with aspirational vs. prohibitory character
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because 51A(j) is aspirational and forward-looking, making students question whether it 'belongs' with 51A(h) and 51A(b) in the aspirational category, without recognising that the odd one out is 51A(i) for being prohibitory/protective.
elimination_logic: Article 51A(b) — cherish noble ideals of the freedom struggle — is aspirational and historically oriented; no specific prohibition involved.
Article 51A(h) — develop scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry — is aspirational and intellectually oriented; no specific prohibition.
Article 51A(j) — strive towards excellence in individual and collective activity — is aspirational and performance-oriented; forward-looking, no prohibition.

Article 51A(i) — safeguard public property AND abjure violence — is prohibitory/protective in character; 'abjure violence' is a formal renunciation, not an aspiration. This is the odd one out among purely aspirational duties — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is partial-truth: all four duties share a civic character, making it tempting to see them as equivalent. The distinguishing criterion — aspirational vs. prohibitory — requires knowing that 51A(i) contains two prohibition-style obligations (safeguard public property, abjure violence), while 51A(b), (h), and (j) are purely forward-looking aspirational duties with no specific prohibition or protective instruction.
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Duties can be broadly classified as aspirational (forward-looking obligations to strive, develop, or cherish) and prohibitory/protective (obligations to refrain from or safeguard against harm).

• Option (a) — Article 51A(b): Aspirational — citizens are urged to cherish and follow the noble ideals of the freedom struggle. No specific prohibition or protective directive.
• Option (b) — Article 51A(h): Aspirational — citizens are directed to develop scientific temper, humanism, and spirit of inquiry and reform. Purely positive in character.
• Option (c) — Article 51A(i): The odd one out. Contains TWO distinct obligations: (i) safeguard public property (protective) and (ii) abjure violence (prohibitory — 'abjure' means to formally renounce). This is not purely aspirational.
• Option (d) — Article 51A(j): Aspirational — citizens must strive towards excellence so the nation rises to higher levels. Forward-looking and performance-oriented.

Value Addition:
• Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984 enforces the first limb of 51A(i).
• 'Abjure' is a precise legal-moral term — it means to solemnly renounce, not merely avoid.
• The Supreme Court in Re: Destruction of Public Property (2009) issued detailed guidelines invoking 51A(i).

solution.concept_anchor: FDs can justify restrictions but cannot override Fundamental Rights

statement_analysis.statement: A law enacted by Parliament to enforce a Fundamental Duty can be used to justify a reasonable restriction on a Fundamental Right under Article 19, provided the restriction satisfies the test of proportionality.
statement_analysis.reason: Courts have held that FDs provide constitutional backing to laws that restrict freedoms in the interest of duties like protecting sovereignty (51A(c)) or the environment (51A(g)) — these align with the permissible grounds under Article 19(2) through (6).

statement_analysis.statement: Fundamental Duties have a constitutional precedence over Fundamental Rights in the same manner that Article 31C gave Directive Principles precedence over Articles 14 and 19.
statement_analysis.reason: There is NO precedence clause for Fundamental Duties — unlike Article 31C (which attempted to shield DPSP-implementing laws from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, partially struck down in Minerva Mills), FDs carry no such override provision; they cannot supersede Part III rights.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 1 is correct may assume Statement 2 is also correct by extending the logic of 31C to FDs, especially since both DPSPs and FDs are non-justiciable.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Laws enforcing FDs can justify restrictions on FRs under Article 19 — this is constitutionally established; courts have upheld such restrictions when they align with grounds in Article 19(2)–(6). Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: There is no Article 31C-equivalent for Fundamental Duties — no constitutional provision gives FDs precedence over Part III rights; the Minerva Mills case specifically limited even the DPSP-FR precedence clause. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap extends the logic of Article 31C (DPSP precedence over FRs) to Fundamental Duties. Students who know that DPSPs and FDs are both non-justiciable and both non-Part III provisions may assume they enjoy similar constitutional treatment. They do not — Article 31C was a specific, contested, and partially struck down provision applying only to DPSPs, and no parallel provision exists for FDs.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Fundamental Duties and Fundamental Rights is complementary, not hierarchical.

• Statement 1 — Correct: FDs can serve as constitutional backing for laws that restrict Fundamental Rights. For example, a law restricting certain speech in the interest of national integrity (aligned with 51A(c)) can be justified under Article 19(2). Courts treat FDs as interpretive anchors when assessing the reasonableness of restrictions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no Article 31C-equivalent for Fundamental Duties. Article 31C gave DPSPs a qualified precedence over Articles 14 and 19 (partially struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India, 1980). Fundamental Duties enjoy no such precedence — they cannot override Part III rights, and no constitutional provision says otherwise.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills (1980) is the landmark case limiting the scope of Article 31C and reaffirming FR supremacy.
• FDs and FRs must be read harmoniously — neither cancels the other.
• The Supreme Court in AIR India v. Nargesh Mirza noted that FDs and FRs are part of an integrated constitutional scheme.

solution.concept_anchor: Verma Committee vs. Swaran Singh Committee — distinct roles
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the Swaran Singh Committee is the more famous of the two and students confuse its role (recommending the insertion of FDs) with the Verma Committee's role (identifying existing laws implementing FDs).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) was set up to recommend the inclusion of FDs in the Constitution — it did not review existing legislation implementing FDs.

Eliminate (c): The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC, 2000–2002, chaired by Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah) reviewed the Constitution broadly — it was not specifically tasked with cataloguing FD-implementing laws.
Eliminate (d): The Second Administrative Reforms Commission was concerned with administrative reforms, not specifically with identifying existing laws on Fundamental Duties.
Confirm (b): Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) was specifically constituted to identify laws already implementing FDs and to suggest awareness measures — this matches the blank precisely.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces the Verma Committee with the Swaran Singh Committee, which is the more commonly studied committee in the FD context. Students who have only superficially covered this topic will default to 'Swaran Singh' for any FD-related committee question. The Verma Committee (1999) had a completely different mandate — retrospective identification of implementing legislation rather than prospective recommendation of FD inclusion.
solution.final_explanation:
Two committees are critical to Fundamental Duties history, and they must not be confused.

• Option (a) — Swaran Singh Committee: Constituted in 1976 to recommend inclusion of a chapter on citizen duties in the Constitution. Its recommendations led to the 42nd Amendment. It did NOT review existing implementing legislation.
• Option (b) — Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999): The correct answer. This committee was specifically tasked with (i) identifying laws already in existence that implement FDs, and (ii) recommending ways to raise citizen awareness about FDs. It found that several laws (Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, Wildlife Protection Act, Environment Protection Act, etc.) already operationalise FDs.
• Option (c) — NCRWC: Reviewed the Constitution's working broadly; not specifically mandated for FD-implementing law cataloguing.
• Option (d) — Second ARC: Focused on administrative governance reforms; no specific FD mandate.

Value Addition:
• The Verma Committee recommended incorporating FDs in school and college curricula.
• No standalone 'FD Enforcement Act' was recommended by either committee — piecemeal legislation was found sufficient.
• The Verma Committee's work connects to National Education Policy debates on civic education.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places the year 1971 with the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act (actually 1984) in option (b). Students who know both statutes exist but have not precisely memorised their enactment years will select this. Additionally, option (c) swaps the statute associated with 51A(g) to 51A(a), exploiting the common tendency to loosely associate 'wildlife' laws with 'national honour' provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
Identifying which statute enforces which Fundamental Duty requires clause-level and year-level precision.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 51A(a) (duty to respect national symbols) is correctly linked to the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. But pairing 51A(i) with this Act is wrong — 51A(i) concerns public property and abjuring violence, not national honour.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act was enacted in 1984, not 1971. This is a year-swap trap.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 operationalises Article 51A(g) (environment/wildlife duty), not 51A(a) (national symbols duty).
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 51A(g) (duty to protect and improve natural environment) is correctly paired with the Environment Protection Act, 1986 — this was specifically identified by the Verma Committee as an existing law implementing this FD.

Value Addition:

• The Verma Committee (1999) catalogued all these linkages.
• No general 'Fundamental Duties Act' exists.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A(d) — no compulsory military conscription
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because the existence of the duty to 'defend the country' leads students to assume it mandates military service, which is the intuitive reading of 'defend.'
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): Article 51A(d) does not mandate compulsory military conscription — India has no law imposing mandatory military service; the duty is conditional ('when called upon') and aspirational.
Eliminate (c): There is no provision in Article 51A(d) restricting this duty to citizens above 18 — the clause does not specify any age threshold.
Eliminate (d): The duty under 51A(d) applies only to citizens, not to all persons within Indian territory.
Confirm (a): The duty has two components — defend the country AND render national service when called upon — making it conditional and dual-natured, not an absolute conscription mandate.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works by converting the conditional duty ('when called upon') into an absolute mandate for compulsory military service. The text of 51A(d) says citizens must 'defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so' — the qualifying phrase 'when called upon' is critical. India has never enacted a compulsory conscription law, and the duty remains aspirational in the absence of such legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A(d) imposes a two-part duty: to defend the country and to render national service when called upon. Both elements are important for the correct characterisation.

• Option (a) — Correct: The duty is dual-natured — it covers both national defence and national service, but the latter is expressly conditional on being 'called upon.' No law mandates compulsory military conscription in India.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 51A(d) does not create an obligation for compulsory military service. India has a voluntary military and no conscription law. Treating 'defend the country' as mandating military enlistment extends the clause beyond its text.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 51A(d) specifies no minimum age — the Constitution does not link this duty to citizens above 18 years.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: All Fundamental Duties are citizen-specific; 51A(d) applies only to citizens, not to all persons on Indian territory.

Value Addition:
• A constitutional debate exists on whether imposing 'national service' could conflict with Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour).
• India's Armed Forces are entirely voluntary — the Agnipath scheme (2022) is voluntary short-service, not conscription.
• 51A(d) is aspirational in the absence of a supporting statute mandating service.

solution.concept_anchor: Precise content of Article 51A(e) — categories and women's dignity clause

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(e) requires every citizen to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood among all people of India, transcending religious, linguistic, regional and sectional diversities.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise text of the first limb of Article 51A(e) — the four specific categories (religious, linguistic, regional, sectional) are constitutionally enumerated.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(e) additionally places a duty on citizens to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women, making it the only Fundamental Duty that directly addresses gender justice.
statement_analysis.reason: The second limb of 51A(e) explicitly addresses renouncing practices derogatory to women's dignity — this is indeed the most direct gender-justice provision among the Fundamental Duties.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(c) requires citizens to uphold sovereignty and unity of India, but does not mention 'integrity' as a separate obligation since integrity is addressed only in the Preamble.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(c) explicitly includes sovereignty, unity, AND integrity as three distinct obligations — 'integrity' appears in both the Preamble and Article 51A(c). Its inclusion in both places was a deliberate design of the 42nd Amendment.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who correctly verify Statements 1 and 2 as true may doubt Statement 3 only partially, recalling that 'integrity' is in the Preamble but unsure whether 51A(c) also includes it, leading them to incorrectly select 'all three.'
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Article 51A(e) lists four precise categories (religious, linguistic, regional, sectional) for harmony; Statement 1 accurately reproduces this — Correct.
Verify Statement 2 — The women's dignity clause in 51A(e) is accurate and it is the most direct gender-justice FD — Correct.
Verify Statement 3 — Article 51A(c) explicitly says 'sovereignty, unity and integrity' — all three terms appear in the duty text; claiming integrity is absent from 51A(c) is false — Incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the tendency to associate 'integrity' exclusively with the Preamble (where it was added by the 42nd Amendment). Students may not recall that the same amendment simultaneously inserted 'integrity' into Article 51A(c). This is a partial-truth trap: the statement correctly says integrity is in the Preamble but falsely implies it is absent from 51A(c).
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 51A(c) and 51A(e) are two of the most content-rich Fundamental Duties, and precise recall of their components is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A(e) mandates promoting harmony transcending four specific categories — religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional diversities. Each category is constitutionally listed and independently testable.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The second limb of 51A(e) requires renouncing practices derogatory to the dignity of women. This is the most explicit gender-justice provision among the FDs and has been invoked in judicial reasoning on sati, triple talaq, and other regressive practices.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 51A(c) includes all three terms — sovereignty, unity, AND integrity. Integrity was added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, both in the Preamble and in Article 51A(c). The claim that integrity appears 'only in the Preamble' is false.

Value Addition:
• 51A(e) connects directly to the Preamble's value of 'fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual.'
• The 42nd Amendment is a pivotal amendment — it added the Preamble words (socialist, secular, integrity), inserted FDs, and restructured several constitutional provisions simultaneously.
• Article 15 (non-discrimination) and 51A(e) together form the constitutional gender-justice framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional source of inspiration for Indian Fundamental Duties

statement_analysis.statement: India's Fundamental Duties were primarily inspired by the Constitution of the USSR (Soviet Union), which was among the few major constitutions to enumerate citizen duties alongside rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The Soviet Constitution is the acknowledged source of inspiration for India's Fundamental Duties — it was the most prominent model at the time that codified citizen obligations alongside rights within the constitutional text.

statement_analysis.statement: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) does not recognize any duty dimension for individuals, confining itself exclusively to enumerating human rights.
statement_analysis.reason: UDHR Article 29 explicitly states that 'everyone has duties to the community in which alone the free and full development of his personality is possible' — the UDHR does acknowledge a duties dimension, though it is not elaborated in detail.

statement_analysis.statement: The Japanese Constitution contains no provision recognizing citizen responsibilities, making India the first Asian democracy to constitutionally enumerate citizen duties.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 12 of the Japanese Constitution contains a responsibility clause — citizens must not abuse rights and must always use them for the public welfare; India is therefore not uniquely the first in this respect.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 1 is correct (USSR inspiration) may assume both Statements 2 and 3 are also incorrect (marking all three as incorrect), but the question format requires at least one correct statement — Statement 1 is correct, making (d): 'all three' the wrong answer.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is factually correct — USSR Constitution inspired Indian FDs; this statement is NOT incorrect.
Statement 2 is factually incorrect — UDHR Article 29 does recognize a duty dimension; this statement IS not correct and qualifies as the answer.
Statement 3 is factually incorrect — Japanese Constitution Article 12 includes citizen responsibility clauses; this statement IS not correct and also qualifies.
Statements 2 and 3 are both NOT correct — select option (a): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common exam shortcut that 'UDHR = rights only.' UDHR Article 29 is rarely tested and students default to characterising it as a rights-only instrument. Statement 3 exploits unfamiliarity with comparative constitutional provisions — the Japanese Article 12 responsibility clause is an obscure but verifiable fact. Both wrong statements sound authoritative, making this a plausible-fabrication-style trap for Statement 3 and scope-extension for Statement 2.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Fundamental Duties exist within a global tradition of constitutions balancing rights with citizen obligations.

• Statement 1 — Correct (NOT the answer): India's FDs were inspired by the USSR Constitution — the Soviet model was notable for enumerating citizen duties alongside rights within a single constitutional document, a feature that influenced the Swaran Singh Committee.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (IS the answer): UDHR Article 29 explicitly recognises that 'everyone has duties to the community.' The UDHR is not purely a rights instrument — it acknowledges the duty-rights balance, though it elaborates duties less extensively than rights.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (IS the answer): Article 12 of the Japanese Constitution requires citizens not to abuse constitutional freedoms and to use them always for the public welfare — this is a clear responsibility clause. India is not uniquely the first Asian democracy with codified citizen duties.

Value Addition:
• German Basic Law also contains provisions on citizen responsibility alongside rights.
• UDHR Article 29 is the international law anchor for the duties-rights balance argument.
• India's FD framework is more detailed than most comparable democratic constitutions — a point relevant for Mains comparative law questions.

Non-Justiciability of Fundamental Duties and Its Exceptions

solution.concept_anchor: DPSP vs. FD — structural distinctions correctly stated

statement_analysis.statement: Both Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable — no court can directly enforce either against the respective duty-bearer.
statement_analysis.reason: DPSPs bind the State but are not enforceable by courts against the State as a direct constitutional claim; similarly, FDs bind citizens but carry no direct judicial remedy for breach — both are non-justiciable in this sense.

statement_analysis.statement: DPSPs are addressed to the State while Fundamental Duties are addressed to citizens — this is the most fundamental structural distinction between the two.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the canonical and most tested distinction — DPSPs (Part IV, Articles 36–51) impose obligations on the State for policy-making; FDs (Part IV-A, Article 51A) impose obligations on individual citizens.

statement_analysis.statement: Directive Principles are contained in Part IV (Articles 36–51) while Fundamental Duties are in Part III alongside Fundamental Rights, reflecting their equal constitutional status.
statement_analysis.reason: Fundamental Duties are NOT in Part III — they are in Part IV-A (a separate part added by the 42nd Amendment). Part III exclusively contains Fundamental Rights. The claim of 'equal constitutional status' is also constitutionally unsupported.

statement_analysis.statement: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended that sanctions be prescribed for breach of Fundamental Duties, but this recommendation was not adopted — FDs remain without a prescribed penalty in the Constitution itself.
statement_analysis.reason: The Committee did recommend sanctions, but the 42nd Amendment did not include any penalty provision for FD breach — the Constitution contains no direct enforcement mechanism, though Parliament can enact supporting legislation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 4 as correct may assume Statement 3 is also correct if they have a vague recollection of FDs being 'near' Fundamental Rights in the Constitution.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — both DPSPs and FDs are non-justiciable in the direct-enforcement sense.
Statement 2 is correct — the state/citizen distinction is the most fundamental structural difference.
Statement 3 is incorrect — FDs are in Part IV-A, NOT Part III; Part III is exclusively for Fundamental Rights.
Statement 4 is correct — Swaran Singh Committee's sanctions recommendation was not adopted.
Three of the four statements are correct — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits geographic imprecision about constitutional placement. Students know FDs are 'related to' rights and are 'near' Part III, leading to the error of placing them in Part III itself. The critical fact is that Part IV-A is a separate constitutional part — not a subsection of Part III or Part IV — created specifically by the 42nd Amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
The structural comparison between DPSPs and FDs is a recurring UPSC Prelims theme.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Neither DPSPs nor FDs are directly enforceable by courts — both operate as moral-constitutional obligations without a direct writ remedy.
• Statement 2 — Correct: DPSPs bind the State (Part IV); FDs bind citizens (Part IV-A). This state/citizen distinction is the most fundamental and frequently tested.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A, not Part III. Part III (Articles 12–35) is exclusively for Fundamental Rights. Placing FDs in Part IV-A was a deliberate constitutional design — separate from both rights and directives, reflecting a distinct constitutional category.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation for sanctions was not implemented. The Constitution imposes no penalty for FD breach — Parliament has enacted supporting statutes (e.g., Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act), but there is no constitutional penalty provision.

Three statements are correct — answer is (c): Only three.

Value Addition:
• Part IV-A has only one article — Article 51A — making it the most compact Part in the Constitution.
• DPSPs (Part IV) include Article 48A on environment; the citizen-facing counterpart is 51A(g) in Part IV-A.
• Both Parts IV and IV-A were significantly shaped by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A(i) — abjure violence and judicial enforcement through guidelines
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Yes. The Supreme Court in Re: Destruction of Public Property (2009) issued detailed guidelines imposing liability on organisers of protests/hartals for damage to public property — this is a verifiable judicial fact.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Yes. Article 51A(i) imposes two obligations: safeguard public property and abjure violence — and 'abjure' specifically means to formally renounce; this is accurate constitutional text.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes. The Supreme Court's guidelines were explicitly anchored in Article 51A(i) — the constitutional duty to safeguard public property and renounce violence provided the normative foundation for imposing organiser liability. R correctly explains why the Court could go beyond mere criminal prosecution to issue proactive liability guidelines.
Both A and R are correct AND R explains A — select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Re: Destruction of Public Property case (2009) is the landmark judicial application of Article 51A(i).

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The Supreme Court, while hearing a PIL on destruction of public property during protests and strikes, issued comprehensive guidelines holding organizers of violent protests vicariously liable for property damage. This was a proactive judicial use of Article 51A(i) beyond ordinary criminal proceedings.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Article 51A(i) contains two distinct obligations — (i) safeguard public property (protective) and (ii) abjure violence (prohibitory). 'Abjure' is precise legal-moral language meaning to formally renounce, not merely avoid.
• Causal Explanation: R correctly explains A. The Court anchored its guidelines in the constitutional duty that citizens must both protect public property and renounce violence. This gave the Court the normative basis to impose organiser liability and establish a rebuttable presumption of damage against protest leaders.

Correct option: (a) — Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• The Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984 (PDPP Act) is the statutory counterpart to 51A(i).
• The Supreme Court's 2009 guidelines also drew on the principle that the right to protest (Article 19) does not include the right to destroy property.
• 'Abjure' is a term students should memorise — it appears only in 51A(i) and has specific legal significance.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A(f) — 'composite' culture is the keyword

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(f) requires citizens to protect and preserve each community's distinct cultural identity, ensuring that no cultural tradition is subsumed into a homogenised national culture.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(f) refers to 'the rich heritage of India's composite culture' — it is about the syncretic, plural whole, not individual communities' distinct identities. Preserving distinct community identities is the subject of Article 29 (Fundamental Right), not Article 51A(f).

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(b), which requires citizens to cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle, is aspirational and moral in character with no existing statute directly enforcing compliance with this duty.
statement_analysis.reason: 51A(b) is purely aspirational — it urges citizens toward historical-ideological commitment; unlike 51A(a) (Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act) or 51A(g) (environmental statutes), no law directly enforces the duty under 51A(b).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students may conflate 51A(f) with Article 29 (right to conserve distinct culture) and assume Statement 1 describes 51A(f) correctly, especially since both provisions relate to cultural heritage.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 51A(f) uses the word 'composite' — it is about India's syncretic cultural heritage as a whole, not individual communities' distinct identities. Statement 1 describes Article 29, not 51A(f). Statement 1 is incorrect.

Evaluate Statement 2: Article 51A(b) is aspirational and moral — no statute directly enforces the duty to cherish freedom struggle ideals. The Verma Committee confirmed no direct enforcement mechanism exists for 51A(b). Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the conceptual proximity between Article 51A(f) (duty to preserve composite culture) and Article 29 (right to conserve distinct culture). The word 'composite' in 51A(f) signals a syncretic, unified cultural heritage — not individual community distinctiveness. Replacing 'composite' with 'distinct' fundamentally changes the obligation. Students unfamiliar with this keyword distinction will accept Statement 1 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The 'composite' vs. 'distinct' distinction is a classic UPSC precision trap between Article 51A(f) and Article 29.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 51A(f) mandates preserving the 'rich heritage of India's composite culture' — 'composite' signals India's syncretic, plural civilizational heritage, not individual community identities. The duty to preserve distinct community cultures falls under the Fundamental Right in Article 29. Conflating the two misreads 51A(f) entirely.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 51A(b) is purely aspirational — citizens are urged to cherish and follow the noble ideals of the freedom struggle. No statute directly enforces this duty; it operates through civic education and moral persuasion. The Verma Committee (1999) did not identify any existing law directly implementing 51A(b).

Value Addition:
• Article 29: Right of minorities to conserve their distinct language, script, or culture — citizen's right, not a duty.
• Article 51A(f): Collective duty to preserve India's syncretic cultural heritage — think of composite culture as the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb, Buddhist-Hindu-Islamic architectural synthesis, etc.
• Courts cite 51A(f) in ASI monument protection disputes and heritage conservation litigation.

solution.concept_anchor: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act — pre-dates Article 51A
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students assume that the legislation enforcing the Article 51A(a) duty must have been enacted after the duty was inserted in 1976, whereas the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act was enacted in 1971 — five years before Article 51A.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act was NOT enacted in 1976 alongside the 42nd Amendment — it predates Article 51A by five years, having been enacted in 1971.
Eliminate (c): The Flag Code of India, 2002 governs the proper display and use of the National Flag — it is a code of conduct, not the primary penal statute for disrespect to national symbols.
Eliminate (d): There is no act called the 'National Symbols Protection Act, 1976' — this is a plausible-fabrication distractor.

Confirm (b): The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 predates Article 51A (inserted in 1976) and operationalises the duty to respect national symbols — it was identified by the Verma Committee as an existing law implementing this FD.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap reverses the chronological relationship between the legislation and the constitutional duty. Students who know the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act is linked to Article 51A(a) naturally assume it was enacted after Article 51A — but it was enacted in 1971, five years before the 42nd Amendment inserted Article 51A. This pre-dating relationship is a frequently tested precision point.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A(a) imposes the duty to abide by the Constitution, respect its ideals and institutions, and respect the National Flag and National Anthem. Parliamentary legislation operationalising this duty exists — and notably predates the duty itself.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act was enacted in 1971, not 1976. Assuming it was enacted simultaneously with Article 51A is a common temporal error.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 is the primary statute linked to Article 51A(a). It criminalises acts of disrespect toward the National Flag, National Anthem, the Constitution, and the map of India. It predates Article 51A by five years — demonstrating that Parliament can enact FD-implementing laws without the FD having first been constitutionally inserted.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Flag Code of India, 2002 is an executive order governing proper use and display of the National Flag — it is not a penal statute for disrespect to national symbols.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No such act as 'National Symbols Protection Act, 1976' exists — a plausible-fabrication distractor.

Value Addition:
• The Bijoe Emmanuel case (1986) interpreted the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act alongside Article 51A(a) and Article 25.
• The Flag Code, 2002 replaced earlier restrictions and allows citizens to fly the Tricolour year-round (amended in 2022 to allow display day and night).
• Pre-existing legislation implementing FDs demonstrates Parliament's sovereign power to enact such laws at any time.

C matches with 4: Article 51A(f) (composite culture) stands in creative tension with Article 29 (right to conserve distinct culture) — the duty on all citizens to preserve composite heritage vs. individual community rights to distinct culture.

D matches with 2: Article 51A(d) (defend country and render national service) raises a constitutional debate with Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour) — can 'national service when called upon' be imposed without violating Article 23?
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap swaps the related constitutional provisions between 51A(d) and 51A(e). Students who know that 51A(e) relates to social harmony may associate it with Article 23 (forced labour) through a vague sense of 'compulsion,' while 51A(d)'s linkage to Article 23 is more precise (the forced labour debate about national service). Option (b) exploits this by correctly placing Bijoe Emmanuel but incorrectly cross-linking the DPSP and rights connections.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests clause-level precision in linking Fundamental Duties to their associated cases and constitutional provisions.

• A–3: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) is the defining case for Article 51A(a). The Supreme Court held that standing respectfully without singing the National Anthem does not breach the duty to respect national symbols — religious conscience (Article 25) was upheld.
• B–1: Article 51A(e) (promoting harmony and brotherhood) is structurally linked to Article 15 (non-discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth) — both address social cohesion and equal dignity in a plural society.
• C–4: Article 51A(f) (composite culture) is in creative tension with Article 29 (right to conserve distinct language, script, or culture). The collective duty to preserve syncretic heritage can conflict with individual community rights to distinct identity.
• D–2: Article 51A(d) (national defence and service when called upon) raises a constitutional tension with Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour and begar). Mandating 'national service' under compulsion could potentially implicate Article 23's prohibitions.

Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → Option (d).

Value Addition:
• Article 25 (freedom of conscience/religion) was the rights provision that overrode the state's enforcement of 51A(a) in Bijoe Emmanuel.
• Article 23 exempts compulsory service for public purposes — but the scope of this exemption in relation to 51A(d) remains a constitutional debate.
• Article 29 is a minority right; Article 51A(f) is a universal citizen duty — their intersection is a Mains-worthy tension.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A(h) — three components: scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(h) imposes a duty to develop not only scientific temper but also humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform — making it a three-component obligation.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional text of 51A(h) explicitly lists three elements: scientific temper, humanism, and spirit of inquiry and reform — all three are independently mandated.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(h) is the only Fundamental Duty with an explicitly intellectual and epistemological character, distinguishing India's constitutional framework from purely civic duty traditions.
statement_analysis.reason: No other FD mandates a mode of thinking or knowing — 51A(h) uniquely targets the intellectual disposition of citizens, reflecting the Nehruvian vision of a modern, rational India.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(b) and Article 51A(j), like Article 51A(h), are purely backward-looking duties — they connect citizens to India's historical past and traditions rather than aspirations for the future.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(j) is explicitly forward-looking — it directs citizens to strive towards excellence so the nation 'constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement.' Calling it backward-looking is factually wrong. 51A(b) is historically oriented but 51A(j) is prospective.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify all three statements as plausible (given the comparative phrasing of Statement 3) may select 'all three' without checking whether 51A(j) is truly backward-looking.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — 51A(h) is a three-part obligation: scientific temper, humanism, and spirit of inquiry and reform. Statement 1 accurately states this — Correct.
Verify Statement 2 — 51A(h) uniquely targets intellectual disposition; no other FD mandates a mode of thinking. Statement 2 is accurate — Correct.
Verify Statement 3 — 51A(j) is explicitly forward-looking ('nation constantly rises to higher levels') — calling it backward-looking is factually wrong; Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 applies a scope-extension error — it correctly characterises 51A(b) as historically oriented but then incorrectly extends the 'backward-looking' label to 51A(j), which is demonstrably prospective. The constitutional text of 51A(j) uses future-tense aspiration language ('constantly rises'), making it unique among FDs as a performance-oriented, forward-looking duty.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A(h)'s three-component structure is a frequent source of exam errors — students often recall only 'scientific temper' and miss 'humanism' and 'spirit of inquiry and reform.'

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A(h) mandates three distinct intellectual obligations: (i) develop scientific temper, (ii) develop humanism, and (iii) develop the spirit of inquiry and reform. Each is independently testable.
• Statement 2 — Correct: 51A(h) is unique in mandating a mode of intellectual engagement — it targets how citizens think and reason. This Nehruvian epistemological imprint distinguishes India's FDs from purely behavioural or civic duties.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 51A(b) is historically and ideologically oriented (freedom struggle ideals) — one could call it backward-looking. But Article 51A(j) is explicitly prospective — it directs citizens to strive for excellence so the nation 'constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement.' It is the most forward-looking of all FDs, not backward-looking.

Value Addition:
• 51A(h)'s 'humanism' component is the most frequently missed element in MCQ traps.
• The Nehruvian vision of scientific temper is captured in the Discovery of India (1946) — relevant Mains context.
• 51A(j) is the constitutional anchor cited in NEP 2020 discussions on excellence in education.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs as interpretive tools — Article 19 restriction reasonableness
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students know FDs are non-justiciable and may conclude that the law cannot be sustained — missing the critical distinction between 'FDs are not directly enforceable' and 'FDs cannot support a restriction on FRs when aligned with Article 19 grounds.'
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Non-justiciability of FDs means citizens cannot be sued for breach of duty — it does not mean FD-aligned legislation cannot restrict Fundamental Rights under Article 19.
Eliminate (b): Fundamental Duties do not have a precedence clause similar to Article 31C — they cannot override Part III rights; this overstates FD authority.

Eliminate (d): The law restricts speech, not religious practice — invoking Article 25 is incorrect in this context. Article 25 governs freedom of conscience and religion, not political speech about territorial integrity.

Confirm (c): A law restricting speech that threatens national integrity can be upheld under Article 19(2) — which permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India. Article 51A(c) provides constitutional backing to such restrictions, reinforcing the reasonableness test.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the scope-extension trap: students extend the non-justiciability of FDs (no direct enforcement against citizens) to mean that FD-aligned laws cannot restrict FRs either. This is wrong — a law restricting speech in the interest of national integrity falls squarely within Article 19(2) grounds, and Article 51A(c) provides the constitutional moral backing. The non-justiciability principle applies to breach-of-duty suits against citizens, not to the validity of parliamentary legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the intersection of Article 51A(c) (sovereignty, unity and integrity duty), Article 19(1)(a) (free speech), and Article 19(2) (reasonable restrictions on free speech).

Parliament enacted a statute that restricts public speech advocating secession of Indian territory, citing it as necessary to protect national integrity. Kavita challenges this under Article 19(1)(a).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Fundamental Duties' non-justiciability means citizens cannot be sued for duty-breach — it does not invalidate parliamentary legislation that restricts speech on grounds aligned with Article 19(2). The two concepts are distinct.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: FDs have no precedence clause over Part III rights (unlike Article 31C for DPSPs). The law must independently satisfy Article 19(2) — FDs support but do not override the rights test.
• Option (c) — Correct: Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India. Article 51A(c) — the duty to uphold sovereignty, unity, and integrity — provides constitutional backing to such legislation, reinforcing the reasonableness determination. Courts can uphold such laws under the Article 19(2) framework.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The law restricts political speech about territory, not religious practice. Article 25 (freedom of religion/conscience) is not the relevant provision here.

Value Addition:
• UAPA (Unlawful Activities Prevention Act) is a real statute linked to sovereignty/integrity — Article 51A(c) is its constitutional moral anchor.
• Article 19(2) grounds: sovereignty, integrity, security of State, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to offence.
• Courts apply a proportionality test when evaluating 19(2) restrictions — Article 51A(c) strengthens the legislative justification.

solution.concept_anchor: Verma Committee findings — which duties have legislative backing

statement_analysis.statement: The Verma Committee (1999) found that no existing legislation operationalised any of the Fundamental Duties — its primary recommendation was for Parliament to enact a comprehensive Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Verma Committee's key finding was the opposite — it identified several EXISTING laws (Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, Wildlife Protection Act, Environment Protection Act, Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act) that already operationalised specific FDs. It did NOT recommend a comprehensive enforcement act.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(b) — the duty to cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle — has a directly enforcing statute in the form of legislation that criminalises misrepresentation of historical events of the Indian independence movement.
statement_analysis.reason: No such statute exists specifically for 51A(b) — this duty remains purely aspirational with no direct enforcement legislation. The Verma Committee did not identify any existing law implementing 51A(b).

statement_analysis.statement: The Verma Committee recommended that awareness about Fundamental Duties be incorporated into school and college curricula as a measure of civic education.
statement_analysis.reason: This was indeed a recommendation of the Verma Committee — it suggested educational integration of FDs as a non-legislative measure to promote civic awareness.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may assume Statement 3 is also wrong (expecting the Committee to recommend only legislative action), missing that the Committee did recommend educational measures.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is factually incorrect — the Verma Committee found EXISTING laws already implementing FDs; it did NOT find a legislative vacuum. This statement IS the answer as 'NOT correct.'
Statement 2 is factually incorrect — no statute criminalises misrepresentation of independence movement history specifically for 51A(b). This statement IS also 'NOT correct.'
Statement 3 is factually correct — the Verma Committee did recommend curricula integration. This is NOT the answer.
Statements 1 and 2 are both NOT correct — select option (b): 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a plausible-fabrication trap — it describes a statute that sounds plausible (criminalising historical misrepresentation) but does not exist. Statement 1 reverses the actual finding of the Verma Committee. Both exploit the tendency of students to have vague knowledge of the Committee's findings, accepting the fabricated inversion or fabricated statute without checking.
solution.final_explanation:
The Verma Committee (1999) had a specific and often misunderstood mandate — it was not tasked with proposing new legislation but with identifying existing laws that already implement FDs.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (IS the answer): The Committee's key finding was that multiple existing statutes already operationalise FDs — Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (51A(a)), Wildlife Protection Act and Environment Protection Act (51A(g)), Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act (51A(i)). It did NOT recommend a comprehensive Fundamental Duties Enforcement Act.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (IS the answer): Article 51A(b) — cherishing freedom struggle ideals — remains entirely aspirational. No statute criminalises misrepresentation of independence movement history specifically to enforce this duty. This is a fabricated pairing.
• Statement 3 — Correct (NOT the answer): The Verma Committee did recommend incorporating FDs into school and college curricula — a soft, educational approach to civic awareness rather than punitive enforcement.

Value Addition:
• The deliberate absence of a general 'FD Enforcement Act' reflects the constitutional choice to keep duties in the moral-civic domain.
• 51A(h) and 51A(j) are among the most 'legislation-free' duties — no statute directly enforces them.
• The Verma Committee's work connects to current debates on civic education in the NEP 2020 framework.

solution.concept_anchor: MC Mehta cases — Article 51A(g) as judicial anchor for environmental duties
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Yes. The Supreme Court in MC Mehta v. Union of India and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India has repeatedly invoked Article 51A(g) to expand environmental obligations on industries and citizens — this is a verifiable fact from landmark environmental jurisprudence.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Yes. Article 51A(g) imposes a two-part citizen duty — protect and improve the natural environment (forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife) AND have compassion for living creatures. This is accurate constitutional text.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes. The Court's invocation of 51A(g) in environmental cases is directly anchored in the constitutional text of 51A(g) — the duty's scope (environment protection) is the normative basis on which courts extended environmental obligations. R correctly explains why courts used 51A(g) as a judicial tool.
Both A and R are correct AND R explains A — select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A(g) has been the most judicially active Fundamental Duty, particularly in environmental law cases.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The Supreme Court has consistently invoked Article 51A(g) in landmark environmental cases — MC Mehta v. Union of India (various), Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) — to impose environmental duties on industries and develop principles like 'polluter pays' and the precautionary principle. This judicial use elevates FDs from pious declarations to active interpretive tools.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Article 51A(g) contains two obligations: (i) protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife; and (ii) have compassion for living creatures. The environmental scope of the provision is constitutionally specified.
• Causal Explanation: R correctly explains A. The courts' environmental jurisprudence is anchored precisely in the scope of 51A(g) — the duty to protect forests, rivers, wildlife provides the constitutional moral foundation for imposing environmental obligations that go beyond ordinary statutory liability. The 'compassion for living creatures' limb also underpins animal welfare decisions.

Correct option: (a) — Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• 51A(g) is the only FD explicitly linked to environmental law — its judicial use is unmatched among FD provisions.
• The 'polluter pays' and 'precautionary principle' in Indian environmental law trace partly to 51A(g).
• Article 48A (DPSP, state duty) and 51A(g) (FD, citizen duty) together form India's constitutional environmental framework.

solution.concept_anchor: 86th Amendment — simultaneous insertion of Article 21A and 51A(k)

statement_analysis.statement: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making the right to free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children between the ages of six and fourteen.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002 — this is the constitutional provision granting every child between 6 and 14 years the right to free and compulsory education.

statement_analysis.statement: The same 86th Amendment simultaneously added clause (k) to Article 51A, imposing on every citizen who is a parent or guardian the duty to provide educational opportunities to their child or ward in the 6–14 age group.
statement_analysis.reason: The 86th Amendment inserted both Article 21A and clause (k) of Article 51A in a single constitutional amendment, creating a rights-duties triangulation alongside Article 45 (DPSP).

statement_analysis.statement: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 was enacted simultaneously with the 86th Amendment in 2002 to give immediate legislative effect to the newly inserted Article 21A.
statement_analysis.reason: The RTE Act was enacted in 2009 — seven years after the 86th Amendment (2002). The two events were not simultaneous; the Act came into force on April 1, 2010.

statement_analysis.statement: The 86th Amendment also amended Article 45 (DPSP), shifting the state's obligation for early childhood care from the 6–14 age group (now covered by Article 21A) to children below the age of six.
statement_analysis.reason: The 86th Amendment amended Article 45 to extend DPSP coverage to early childhood care and education for children below six, completing the constitutional framework for education across all age groups.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor: students who correctly assess three statements as correct but assume the RTE Act's simultaneous enactment is also true will select 'All four' — the temporal gap between 2002 (amendment) and 2009 (Act) is the critical distinction.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — Article 21A inserted by 86th Amendment, 2002; age group 6–14 is accurate.
Statement 2 is correct — Clause (k) was added by the same 86th Amendment; parental duty for children aged 6–14.
Statement 3 is incorrect — RTE Act was enacted in 2009, not 2002; the two were NOT simultaneous.
Statement 4 is correct — Article 45 was amended by the 86th Amendment to redirect DPSP coverage to children below 6.
Three of four statements are correct — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits a temporal-swap: the constitutional amendment (2002) and the implementing legislation (2009) are seven years apart. Students who know both events are linked to Article 21A often assume they occurred simultaneously, especially since the question presents the year 2002 for the Act as if it coincides with the amendment. This is one of the most common year-based errors in FD-related questions.
solution.final_explanation:
The 86th Constitutional Amendment, 2002 is a pivotal three-pronged intervention in education law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 21A grants children between 6 and 14 years the Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education — inserted by the 86th Amendment.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Clause (k) was simultaneously added to Article 51A by the same amendment, creating a corresponding parental duty for the same age group — a rights-duties pair engineered within a single amendment.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act was enacted in 2009, not 2002. The seven-year gap between constitutional insertion and legislative operationalisation is a commonly tested factual distinction. The RTE Act came into force on April 1, 2010.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The 86th Amendment also modified Article 45 — the original DPSP targeted education up to age 14; after the amendment, Article 45 focuses on early childhood care and education for children below six years, while Article 21A handles the 6–14 group.

Only three statements are correct — answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The 86th Amendment created a constitutional triangle: Article 21A (right on child), Article 51A(k) (duty on parent), Article 45 DPSP (obligation on State for under-6).
• RTE Act, 2009 applies to children aged 6–14 — mirrors the constitutional age group in Article 21A.
• India's universal elementary education framework is built on this 2002–2009 constitutional-legislative sequence.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronological enactment of FD-implementing statutes
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students may correctly place the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) first but then confuse the relative order of the Environment Protection Act (1986) and the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act (1984).
elimination_logic: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act — enacted 1971; this is the earliest and predates Article 51A itself.
Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act — enacted 1984; this came after Article 51A was inserted in 1976.
Environment Protection Act — enacted 1986; this came after the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act (1984).
Correct order: 1971 → 1984 → 1986, i.e., National Honour Act → Public Property Act → Environment Protection Act — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap reverses the 1984 and 1986 statutes. Students who know the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act is earliest (1971) may not have precise recall of whether the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act (1984) or the Environment Protection Act (1986) came next. Option (b) exploits this by reversing these two, offering the plausible-looking sequence: 1971 → 1986 → 1984.
solution.final_explanation:
Three key statutes operationalise specific Fundamental Duties, and their chronological sequence tests year-level precision.

• Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971: Linked to Article 51A(a) — the earliest of the three; notably predates the insertion of Article 51A by five years (42nd Amendment was in 1976). This Act criminalises disrespect to the National Flag, National Anthem, and the Constitution.
• Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984: Linked to Article 51A(i) — enacted during Rajiv Gandhi's government in the aftermath of anti-Sikh violence; invoked by the Supreme Court in Re: Destruction of Public Property (2009) guidelines.
• Environment Protection Act, 1986: Linked to Article 51A(g) — enacted two years after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) as a comprehensive umbrella legislation for environmental protection; frequently invoked alongside the Wildlife Protection Act (1972) in environmental cases.

Correct order: 1971 → 1984 → 1986 — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 also operationalises 51A(g) — it predates the Environment Protection Act.
• The Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984) was a direct impetus for the Environment Protection Act, 1986.
• The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 covers the Constitution, the National Flag, and the National Anthem — three separate subjects in one act.
