solution.concept_anchor: Citizen-specific rights parallel to citizen-specific FDs
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students may confuse Article 30 (right of minorities to establish educational institutions) with Article 29 (right to conserve distinct culture) — both are minority-rights provisions and both are citizen-specific, but the distinction between them is subtle.
elimination_logic: Article 15 (prohibition of discrimination) — citizen-specific right; applies only to citizens. Belongs in the citizen-specific category.
Article 19 (freedom of speech, assembly, movement, etc.) — citizen-specific right; applies only to citizens. Belongs in the citizen-specific category.
Article 29 (right to conserve distinct culture/language/script) — citizen-specific right. Belongs in the category.
Article 14 (equality before law and equal protection) — applies to 'any person'; it is NOT citizen-specific. This is the odd one out.
Select option (b): Article 14 does not belong with the citizen-specific rights.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the concept of 'fundamental rights' with 'citizen-specific rights.' Students know all four are in Part III but may not recall which extend to all persons and which are citizen-specific. Article 14 uses the language 'any person' and is universally applicable — a key distinction that makes it the odd one out in a group of citizen-specific rights. This is also the parallel cited in the key dimension for FDs' citizen-specific applicability.
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Rights are not uniformly citizen-specific — some extend to all persons while others are limited to citizens. This distinction has direct structural parallel with Fundamental Duties (which are entirely citizen-specific).

• Option (a) — Article 15: Citizen-specific. Prohibits discrimination by the State against any citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
• Option (b) — Article 14: The odd one out. The right to equality before law and equal protection of laws uses the phrase 'any person' — it applies to citizens, foreigners, and corporations. It is NOT citizen-specific.
• Option (c) — Article 19: Citizen-specific. The six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession) are available only to citizens.
• Option (d) — Article 29: Citizen-specific. The right of any section of citizens to conserve their distinct language, script, or culture is a citizens-only right.

Value Addition:
• Articles applicable to 'all persons' (not just citizens): 14, 20, 21, 22, 25, 27, 28.
• Articles exclusive to citizens: 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs and DPSPs — non-justiciability, duty-bearer, and precedence distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: Both Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles are non-justiciable, but while DPSPs direct the State to achieve certain policy goals, Fundamental Duties direct citizens toward certain behaviours and attitudes.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the most fundamental and accurate structural distinction — DPSPs impose obligations on the State for policy-making, while FDs impose obligations on citizens; both categories are non-justiciable.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 31C of the Constitution, which protects certain DPSP-implementing laws from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, applies equally to laws implementing Fundamental Duties.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 31C was enacted specifically for DPSPs — it has no extension to Fundamental Duties. The Minerva Mills case (1980) further limited Article 31C's scope. No parallel provision exists for FD-implementing laws.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Part IV (DPSPs) and Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties) were present in the original Constitution of India as adopted in 1950.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IV (DPSPs) was in the original Constitution; Part IV-A was NOT — it was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. The original Constitution had no Fundamental Duties chapter.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as true may recall that 'both DPSPs and FDs were part of the constitutional drafting discussions' and assume they were both in the original Constitution, making Statement 3 appear plausible.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — DPSPs bind the State; FDs bind citizens; both are non-justiciable. This is textbook constitutional law — Correct.
Verify Statement 2 — Article 31C was designed exclusively for DPSPs, not FDs; the Minerva Mills case confirmed this. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — Part IV-A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976; it was NOT in the original 1950 Constitution. Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (c): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap: Part IV (DPSPs) was indeed original, but students who recall 'both DPSPs and FDs are in the Constitution' may conflate their origins and assume both were original provisions. Statement 2 exploits the common exam conflation of 'DPSP laws' and 'FD-implementing laws' — Article 31C specifically covers the former, not the latter.
solution.final_explanation:
The structural comparison between DPSPs and FDs requires clarity on three dimensions: justiciability, duty-bearer identity, and constitutional origin.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Both DPSPs (Part IV) and FDs (Part IV-A) are non-justiciable — but DPSPs direct the State toward policy goals while FDs direct citizens toward civic behaviours. This is the canonical and most testable distinction.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 31C was enacted to protect DPSP-implementing laws from challenges under Articles 14 and 19. It has no application to Fundamental Duties. The Minerva Mills case (1980) even clipped Article 31C's scope — extending it to FDs would require a separate constitutional provision that does not exist.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Part IV (DPSPs, Articles 36–51) was in the original Constitution adopted on November 26, 1949. Part IV-A was NOT — the original Constitution contained no Fundamental Duties. Part IV-A with Article 51A was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

Value Addition:
• The original Constitution borrowed DPSPs from the Irish Constitution (influenced by the Spanish Constitution of 1931).
• India's FDs were the only major post-adoption addition to the constitutional framework of fundamental values.
• The B.R. Ambedkar-led Constituent Assembly did not include FDs — they were a 1976 political decision during the Emergency period.

solution.concept_anchor: Correct pairing of FD clause with its constitutional character
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly pairs 51A(h) with 'epistemological' but swaps 51A(b) and 51A(f), exploiting the thematic proximity between historical-cultural heritage (b) and composite cultural preservation (f).
elimination_logic: A matches with 2: Article 51A(b) — cherishing freedom struggle ideals — is historical and ideological in character; it looks backward to the independence movement for moral guidance.
B matches with 4: Article 51A(f) — preserving composite culture — is syncretic and civilizational; it concerns India's plural cultural heritage as a whole, using 'composite' as the key word.
C matches with 1: Article 51A(h) — scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry — is epistemological; it targets the intellectual and rational disposition of citizens uniquely among all FDs.
D matches with 3: Article 51A(j) — striving for excellence — is performative and prospective; it is the only forward-looking, achievement-oriented duty.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap occurs between 51A(b) (historical/ideological) and 51A(f) (syncretic/civilizational). Both relate to heritage and values — (b) is about the freedom movement's ideals while (f) is about India's composite cultural tradition. Students who conflate 'heritage' across both articles will misplace them. The correct association requires knowing that (b) is specifically about the independence movement while (f) is about civilizational plurality.
solution.final_explanation:
Classifying Fundamental Duties by their constitutional character requires going beyond the duty's subject matter to its underlying orientation.

• A–2: Article 51A(b) — Historical/ideological: Citizens must cherish and follow the noble ideals of the Indian freedom struggle. This duty looks backward to the independence movement as a moral touchstone.
• B–4: Article 51A(f) — Syncretic/civilizational: Citizens must preserve India's 'composite culture' — the plural, syncretic tradition that has developed across centuries of India's civilizational history. 'Composite' is the operative keyword.
• C–1: Article 51A(h) — Epistemological: Citizens must develop scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform. This is the only FD that targets a mode of thinking and knowing — an intellectual orientation unique among all 11 duties.
• D–3: Article 51A(j) — Performative/prospective: Citizens must strive towards excellence so the nation constantly rises — this is the only explicitly future-oriented, achievement-linked duty.

Correct: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 → Option (b).

Value Addition:
• 51A(h)'s epistemological character reflects Nehru's vision of India as a rational, modern state — articulated in Discovery of India.
• 51A(j) is cited in NEP 2020 as the constitutional basis for excellence in education.
• The 'composite culture' of 51A(f) differs from 'distinct culture' of Article 29 — the former is about civilizational synthesis, the latter about community-specific preservation.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs as aids to statutory interpretation — non-justiciable but not irrelevant

statement_analysis.statement: A citizen who fails to develop scientific temper as required by Article 51A(h) or who does not cherish the freedom struggle's ideals as required by Article 51A(b) cannot be prosecuted or penalised on the sole basis of breaching those constitutional duties.
statement_analysis.reason: FDs are non-justiciable — there is no direct legal remedy for breach of any Fundamental Duty; a citizen cannot be prosecuted solely for failing to develop scientific temper or for not cherishing freedom struggle ideals. No statute prescribes such offences.

statement_analysis.statement: Courts have held that Fundamental Duties are constitutionally irrelevant and play no role in the interpretation of statutes, determination of reasonableness of restrictions on Fundamental Rights, or filling gaps in constitutional reasoning.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the classic scope-extension error — courts have explicitly used Article 51A as an interpretive tool in MC Mehta, Bijoe Emmanuel, and AIIMS Students Union cases. FDs are not constitutionally irrelevant; they serve interpretive, gap-filling, and reasonableness-determining functions in adjudication.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know FDs are non-justiciable may assume both statements align with that principle — accepting Statement 2's characterisation of 'irrelevance' as a logical extension of non-justiciability.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Citizens cannot be prosecuted solely for breaching 51A(h) or 51A(b) — no statute creates such offences; FDs lack direct enforceability. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Courts have repeatedly used Article 51A as an interpretive tool and reasonableness anchor — the characterisation of FDs as 'constitutionally irrelevant' is factually wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 extends the non-justiciability of FDs into a claim of constitutional irrelevance — this is the most dangerous exam error in this topic. Non-justiciability means 'no direct judicial enforcement against citizens for breach.' It does not mean courts cannot use Article 51A in their reasoning. The distinction between enforceability and relevance is the core conceptual test of this question.
solution.final_explanation:
The non-justiciability of Fundamental Duties has precise boundaries that students must understand.

• Statement 1 — Correct: No citizen can be prosecuted or penalised solely for failing to perform a Fundamental Duty — whether it is developing scientific temper (51A(h)) or cherishing freedom struggle ideals (51A(b)). No statute creates such offences for these aspirational duties. Non-justiciability is real and operative.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Non-justiciability ≠ constitutional irrelevance. Courts have actively used Article 51A: (i) in MC Mehta to impose environmental duties (51A(g)); (ii) in Bijoe Emmanuel to define the limits of enforcing national symbol respect (51A(a)); (iii) in AIIMS Students Union to support merit-based policies (51A(j)); and (iv) generally to assess the reasonableness of restrictions under Article 19. Declaring FDs 'constitutionally irrelevant' fundamentally mischaracterises the judicial record.

Value Addition:
• The test to remember: FDs cannot be enforced AGAINST citizens directly, but courts can use them FOR citizens or for interpretive purposes.
• The Verma Committee (1999) specifically highlighted this dual character — moral non-enforceability alongside judicial utility.
• FDs can fill 'constitutional gaps' when no explicit provision addresses an issue — a tool of judicial interpretation.

solution.concept_anchor: USSR as the source of inspiration for Indian Fundamental Duties
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Ireland is the acknowledged source of India's DPSP framework, and students who know this may over-apply it to FDs as well, since both DPSPs and FDs are non-justiciable citizen/state obligations.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): The Irish Constitution is the source of India's Directive Principles of State Policy — not Fundamental Duties. Confusing the two is a classic entity-swap error.
Eliminate (c): The French Constitution is associated with the Preamble's 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity' influence and the republican ideals — not specifically with codified citizen duties.
Eliminate (d): The American Constitution is the source of India's Fundamental Rights framework (judicial review, bill of rights tradition) — not Fundamental Duties.

Confirm (a): India's Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the USSR (Soviet Union) — the most prominent major constitution at the time that codified citizen duties alongside rights within the constitutional text.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces USSR with Ireland — both are cited in the context of India's constitutional borrowings, but for completely different provisions. Ireland → DPSPs. USSR → Fundamental Duties. Students who have memorised 'Ireland = non-justiciable constitutional provisions' without distinguishing DPSPs from FDs will select option (b). The USSR connection is specific to the concept of codified citizen duties within a constitutional document.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Constitution is renowned for drawing inspiration from multiple constitutional models across the world. The source for each provision matters for precision.

• Option (a) — Correct: The USSR (Soviet Union) Constitution was the primary inspiration for India's Fundamental Duties. The Soviet model was notable for listing citizen duties alongside rights within the constitutional text — a feature adopted by the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation and the 42nd Amendment.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Irish Constitution (Bunreacht na hÉireann) is the source of India's Directive Principles of State Policy — not Fundamental Duties. Both are non-justiciable obligations, but one is directed at the State (DPSP from Ireland) and the other at citizens (FDs from USSR).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The French Constitution influenced India's ideals of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity in the Preamble. It was not the specific source for the codified citizen duties framework.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The American Constitution is the primary inspiration for India's Fundamental Rights (judicial review, bill of rights tradition), not for Fundamental Duties.

Value Addition:
• Key borrowings: UK → Parliamentary democracy, rule of law; USA → FRs, judicial review; Ireland → DPSPs; USSR → FDs; Australia → Concurrent List, trade/commerce; Canada → Federation with strong Centre.

solution.concept_anchor: Precise textual components of selected FD clauses

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(e) requires citizens to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women as one of its two distinct obligations.
statement_analysis.reason: 51A(e) has two components: (i) promote harmony and spirit of common brotherhood transcending religious, linguistic, regional and sectional diversities, and (ii) renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(f) requires citizens to protect and promote India's diverse regional cultures individually, ensuring that each state's cultural traditions are preserved separately.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(f) requires preserving India's 'composite culture' — the syncretic, plural whole — not individual regional cultures separately. Separate preservation of distinct cultures is the subject of Article 29, not 51A(f).

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(g) is the only Fundamental Duty that explicitly covers both an environmental obligation AND a duty of compassion toward living creatures.
statement_analysis.reason: 51A(g) uniquely combines two obligations: protect and improve the natural environment (forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife) AND have compassion for living creatures — no other FD clause has this dual structure covering environmental law and animal welfare simultaneously.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(i) requires citizens to 'abjure' violence — meaning to formally renounce it — which is a stronger obligation than merely refraining from violent acts.
statement_analysis.reason: 'Abjure' means to formally and solemnly renounce — it implies a positive commitment to non-violence, not merely passive avoidance. This is a precise textual distinction that courts and scholars have noted.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who identify Statements 1, 3, and 4 as correct and Statement 2 as incorrect might miscalculate and select 'Only three' without re-verifying, which is in fact the correct answer — making (c) both the strong distractor AND the correct answer.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — 51A(e) has two parts; the women's dignity clause is the second. Confirmed.
Statement 2 is incorrect — 51A(f) is about 'composite culture' (the syncretic whole), not individual regional cultures preserved separately. Rejected.
Statement 3 is correct — 51A(g) uniquely combines environmental duty and compassion for living creatures. Confirmed.
Statement 4 is correct — 'abjure' means formal renunciation, a stronger standard than mere avoidance. Confirmed.
Three of four statements are correct — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 applies a scope-extension to Article 51A(f) by substituting 'composite culture' (the constitutional text) with 'individual regional cultures' (what Article 29 actually covers). Students who know 51A(f) is about cultural preservation but have not memorised the word 'composite' will accept Statement 2 as a reasonable paraphrase — which it is not. The word 'composite' signals civilizational synthesis, not regional pluralism.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise textual knowledge of four distinct Fundamental Duty clauses.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 51A(e) has two obligations — (i) promote harmony and brotherhood across religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional diversities, and (ii) renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity. Both limbs are independently testable.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 51A(f) mandates preserving India's 'composite culture' — the syncretic, plural civilizational heritage as a unified whole. It does not require separate preservation of individual regional cultures, which falls under Article 29 (a Fundamental Right). This is the most frequently missed distinction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 51A(g) uniquely covers two domains — environmental protection (forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife) and compassion for living creatures. No other FD combines environmental law with animal welfare in this way.
• Statement 4 — Correct: 'Abjure' is a precise legal-moral term meaning to formally renounce. The duty to abjure violence is more demanding than an obligation to merely avoid violence — it requires a positive commitment to non-violence.

Three of four statements are correct — answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The 'compassion for living creatures' limb of 51A(g) underlies India's animal welfare jurisprudence.
• 'Composite culture' is a judicial citation in ASI monument protection and heritage conservation cases.
• Article 29's 'distinct culture' vs. 51A(f)'s 'composite culture' is a classic paired Prelims trap.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A(k) — duty on parents, right on children, obligation on State
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly states that the duty under 51A(k) falls on parents — which is true — but incorrectly assigns the corresponding right to the parent rather than the child, conflating the duty-bearer with the right-holder.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The corresponding constitutional RIGHT is on the CHILD (Article 21A), not on the parent. Parents are duty-bearers, not right-holders in this triangle.
Eliminate (b): The age group in Article 51A(k) and Article 21A is 6–14 years, not 6–18 years. The upper limit is 14, not 18.

Eliminate (d): The State's obligation under the RTE Act framework is to PROVIDE free and compulsory education — Article 51A(k) imposes the duty on parents/guardians to PROVIDE OPPORTUNITIES. The pairing of 51A(k) with 'state obligation under RTE' misattributes the duty-bearer.

Confirm (c): Article 51A(k) is correctly described as imposing a duty on citizen-parents/guardians to provide educational opportunities for children/wards between 6 and 14 years — and this duty is complemented by, but distinct from, Article 21A (child's right) and the RTE Act (state obligation).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the three-way relationship between the duty (on parents, 51A(k)), the right (on children, Article 21A), and the State obligation (under RTE Act). Option (a) conflates duty-bearer and right-holder; option (d) conflates the parent's duty with the State's obligation. The question rewards understanding the precise three-party architecture created by the 86th Amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 51A(k) is best understood through its three-way constitutional architecture.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The parent holds the constitutional DUTY under 51A(k) — but the corresponding RIGHT to free education belongs to the CHILD under Article 21A. Calling it 'the parent's constitutional right to ensure education' conflates duty-bearer with right-holder.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The age group in both Article 21A and Article 51A(k) is 6 to 14 years. The claim of '6 to 18 years' is factually wrong — 18 would extend the obligation well beyond what the Constitution provides.
• Option (c) — Correct: Article 51A(k) imposes on every citizen who is a parent or guardian the duty to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years. This is a citizen-specific, role-based, non-justiciable constitutional duty — accurately described in this pair.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The RTE Act creates obligations primarily on the State and educational institutions to provide free schooling — not on parents under 51A(k). The duty in 51A(k) is on parents; the obligation under RTE is on the State apparatus.

Value Addition:
• Article 21A: Child's fundamental right — enforceable against the State.
• Article 51A(k): Parent's constitutional duty — non-justiciable directly but supported by RTE Act framework.
• Article 45 (as amended by 86th Amendment): State's DPSP duty for children below 6 years.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(a) specifically includes a duty to 'respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem' but does NOT include a duty to 'abide by the Constitution' — the abiding duty is addressed separately in the Preamble.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A(a) contains THREE components: (i) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, (ii) respect the National Flag, and (iii) respect the National Anthem. The duty to 'abide by the Constitution' is explicitly included in 51A(a) itself, not merely in the Preamble.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(c) requires citizens to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India — but does NOT include 'independence' as a separate constitutionally listed obligation under this clause.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional text of 51A(c) lists precisely three terms: sovereignty, unity, and integrity. 'Independence' is not a separate listed obligation under this clause, even though it is conceptually related to sovereignty.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 51A(e) mentions four specific categories of diversity that citizens must transcend in promoting brotherhood — but 'economic' and 'caste' diversities are among those four categories.
statement_analysis.reason: The four categories listed in 51A(e) are: religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional diversities. 'Economic' and 'caste' are NOT among the enumerated categories — this is a scope-extension error.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may assume Statement 3 is correct — 'caste' is a prominent discrimination category in Indian law (Article 15) and students may assume it must appear in the brotherhood-promoting duty.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is factually incorrect — 51A(a) explicitly includes 'abide by the Constitution' as the first of three components; this statement IS 'not correct.'
Statement 2 is factually correct — 51A(c) lists sovereignty, unity, and integrity; 'independence' is not separately enumerated; this statement is NOT the answer.
Statement 3 is factually incorrect — the four categories in 51A(e) are religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional; 'economic' and 'caste' are absent; this statement IS 'not correct.'
Statements 1 and 3 are both NOT correct — select option (d): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 applies scope-extension by inserting 'caste' and 'economic' into the specific list enumerated in Article 51A(e). 'Caste' is prominently listed in Article 15 (non-discrimination) and Article 16 (equal opportunity), making it feel natural to assume it appears in the brotherhood-promoting duty. But 51A(e) lists only four categories: religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional — and these must be memorised precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
Precision in identifying what IS and what is NOT included in specific Fundamental Duty clauses is a hallmark UPSC question design.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (IS the answer): Article 51A(a) has three components: (i) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, (ii) respect the National Flag, and (iii) respect the National Anthem. The claim that 'abide by the Constitution' is absent from 51A(a) and relegated to the Preamble is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Correct (NOT the answer): Article 51A(c) lists exactly three terms — sovereignty, unity, and integrity. 'Independence' is not a separately enumerated obligation under this clause. This statement accurately reflects the constitutional text.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (IS the answer): The four categories listed in Article 51A(e) for promoting brotherhood are: religious, linguistic, regional, and sectional diversities. 'Economic' and 'caste' do not appear. Inserting them conflates 51A(e) with the language of Articles 15 and 16.

Value Addition:
• 'Sectional' diversity in 51A(e) is broad — it encompasses occupational, social, and other interest-group divisions not specifically named elsewhere.
• The word 'sectional' captures what Articles 15 and 16 call 'place of birth' or 'social group' distinctions without using those specific terms.
• Memorise 51A(e)'s four categories as R-L-R-S: Religious, Linguistic, Regional, Sectional.

solution.final_explanation:
Two committees are essential knowledge for Fundamental Duties, and their years must be precisely recalled.

• Option (a) — 1973: Incorrect. This year is associated with the Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala judgment establishing the basic structure doctrine — unrelated to Fundamental Duties committees.
• Option (b) — 1976: Correct. The Swaran Singh Committee was constituted in 1976, the same year as the 42nd Constitutional Amendment that inserted Article 51A. The Committee recommended incorporating citizen duties — its recommendation was accepted, though modified in details.
• Option (c) — 1999: Incorrect. 1999 is the year of the Justice J.S. Verma Committee, which was tasked with identifying existing laws that implement Fundamental Duties and recommending awareness measures. Swaran Singh and Verma are separate committees with separate years.
• Option (d) — 1978: Incorrect. 1978 is the year of the 44th Constitutional Amendment (Janata government's corrections to Emergency-era changes) — not connected to Swaran Singh Committee proceedings.

Value Addition:
• Swaran Singh (1976): Recommended FDs → Resulted in Article 51A (42nd Amendment, 1976).
• Verma Committee (1999): Reviewed existing FD-implementing laws → Recommended curricular integration.
• The NCRWC (2000–2002, chaired by Justice Venkatachaliah) reviewed the Constitution broadly — a third committee sometimes confused with the Verma Committee.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs as interpretive tools in determining constitutionality of statutes
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because it invokes the DPSP framework (Article 37) which students know is constitutionally relevant to policy adjudication, confusing the DPSP-based analysis with the FD-based interpretive tool in this specific scenario.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): FDs are not 'legally irrelevant' — the scenario involves a court using Article 51A as an interpretive aid, which is a recognised judicial practice.

Eliminate (c): Article 37 is the provision declaring DPSPs non-justiciable but relevant for governance — it applies to DPSPs, not to FDs. The statute here is aimed at implementing a Fundamental Duty, not a DPSP.
Eliminate (d): Fundamental Duties have no precedence clause over Fundamental Rights — they cannot override Part III rights; the court must independently apply Article 19(2) to assess the statute.

Confirm (a): The court can use Article 51A(g) as an interpretive tool to assess the reasonableness of the restriction under Article 19(2). The FD provides constitutional backing to the legislation's purpose without overriding the rights test — this is the established judicial practice.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) conflates the DPSP framework (Article 37) with the FD framework (Article 51A). Students who have studied both know that Article 37 makes DPSPs non-justiciable but relevant for state action — they may mistakenly apply this DPSP logic to a FD-based statute, selecting option (c). The correct analysis uses Article 51A(g) as an interpretive aid within the Article 19(2) reasonableness test — not through Article 37.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the nuanced judicial use of Article 51A as an interpretive anchor in constitutional adjudication.

A state government enacts a law prohibiting industrial discharge into a river basin within its territory, restricting certain commercial activities. An industry association challenges the law under Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of trade/profession). The government argues the law is grounded in both Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty).

• Option (a) — Correct: The court can use Article 51A(g) as an interpretive tool to assess whether the restriction on trade/profession is reasonable under Article 19(6). The FD on environmental protection provides constitutional backing to the legislative intent, reinforcing the reasonableness determination. This is the established judicial approach — FDs are aids to constitutional adjudication.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: FDs are not legally irrelevant — courts have repeatedly used them in environmental and other cases. Dismissing Article 51A(g) as judicially useless mischaracterises its interpretive role.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 37 governs DPSPs — it declares them non-justiciable but relevant for governance. Applying Article 37 to this scenario conflates the DPSP framework with the FD framework.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: FDs have no precedence clause over Fundamental Rights. The court cannot uphold the law simply because it implements a Fundamental Duty — it must satisfy the Article 19(6) test.

Value Addition:
• Article 19(6) permits 'reasonable restrictions' on freedom of trade/profession in the interest of the general public.
• Environmental laws have been consistently upheld using Article 19(6) + Article 51A(g) + Article 48A in combination.
• The MC Mehta line of cases demonstrates this three-provision interpretive framework in action.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly pairs 51A(c) with sovereignty/unity/integrity but swaps 51A(a) and 51A(b), exploiting the thematic proximity between 'national symbols' (a) and 'freedom struggle ideals' (b) — both relate to national identity.
elimination_logic: A matches with 3: Article 51A(a) has three components — abide by the Constitution AND respect its ideals and institutions AND respect the National Flag and National Anthem. This three-part structure is the defining feature of 51A(a).
B matches with 1: Article 51A(b) requires cherishing and following the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom — historical and ideological in character.
C matches with 4: Article 51A(c) is the sovereignty, unity, and integrity duty — three distinct obligations that must all be noted.
D matches with 2: Article 51A(d) requires defending the country AND rendering national service 'when called upon' — the conditional phrase is the defining element of 51A(d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between 51A(a) and 51A(b) exploits their thematic adjacency — both are about national identity, but one is about symbols and institutions while the other is about historical ideals. Students who know both duties in content but have not memorised clause assignments will swap them. The three-part structure of 51A(a) (Constitution + symbols + anthem) and the purely historical character of 51A(b) are the distinguishing features.
solution.final_explanation:
Matching clauses (a) through (d) of Article 51A to their precise content is a test of clause-level memorisation.

• A–3: Article 51A(a) is a three-part duty: (i) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions; (ii) respect the National Flag; and (iii) respect the National Anthem. The three-part structure distinguishes it from all other clauses.
• B–1: Article 51A(b) requires citizens to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national freedom struggle — purely historical and ideological, looking backward to the independence movement.
• C–4: Article 51A(c) mandates upholding and protecting sovereignty, unity, AND integrity of India — all three terms must be present. Omitting any one makes a characterisation incomplete.
• D–2: Article 51A(d) imposes two obligations — defend the country AND render national service 'when called upon to do so.' The conditional phrase 'when called upon' is the critical qualifier that prevents this from becoming a compulsory conscription mandate.

Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → Option (c).

Value Addition:
• Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) is the leading case interpreting 51A(a)'s scope — respectful standing without singing does not breach the duty.
• 51A(d)'s 'when called upon' qualifier is a constitutional safeguard against compulsory military service.
• 51A(c)'s listing of 'integrity' alongside sovereignty and unity links to the 42nd Amendment's simultaneous insertion of 'integrity' in the Preamble.
